content: 1. Routine annual influenza vaccination is recommended for all individuals aged 6 months and older who do not have contraindications to the vaccine. 2. For the 2016-2017 influenza season, inactivated influenza vaccines (IIVs) will be available in both trivalent (IIV3) and quadrivalent (IIV4) formulations. 3. Recombinant influenza vaccine (RIV) will be available in a trivalent formulation (RIV3). 4. Due to concerns about low effectiveness against influenza A (H1N1)pdm09 in the United States during the 2013-2014 and 2015-2016 seasons, the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) has made an interim recommendation that the live attenuated influenza vaccine (LAIV4) should not be used during the 2016-2017 season. 5. The trivalent influenza vaccines for the 2016-2017 season will include an A/California/7/2009 (H1N1)-like virus, an A/Hong Kong/4801/2014 (H3N2)-like virus, and a B/Brisbane/60/2008-like virus (Victoria lineage). 6. Quadrivalent vaccines will include an additional influenza B virus strain, specifically a B/Phuket/3073/2013-like virus (Yamagata lineage). 7. Recommendations for the use of different vaccine types and specific populations are provided in detail. 8. A licensed, age-appropriate influenza vaccine should be used for vaccination. 9. No preferential recommendation is made for one influenza vaccine product over another for individuals for whom more than one licensed, recommended product is appropriate. 10. This information is intended for vaccination providers, immunization program personnel, and public health professionals. 11. Influenza viruses typically circulate widely in the United States annually, from late fall through early spring. 12. While most individuals infected with influenza viruses recover without complications, influenza can cause severe illness and death, particularly among older adults, very young children, pregnant women, and individuals with chronic medical conditions. 13. During 31 influenza seasons from 1976-1977 through 2006-2007, estimated influenza-associated deaths in the United States ranged from approximately 3,300 to 49,000 annually. 14. Annual influenza vaccination is the primary method for preventing influenza and its complications. 15. A variety of influenza vaccine types are available, and abbreviation conventions for these vaccines have evolved over time. 16. For the 2016-2017 season, IIVs as a class will include egg-based, unadjuvanted, and adjuvanted trivalent influenza vaccines (IIV3s), as well as egg-based or cell culture-based unadjuvanted quadrivalent influenza vaccines (IIV4s). 17. RIV refers to recombinant hemagglutinin influenza vaccine, available as a trivalent formulation (RIV3) for the 2016-2017 season. 18. LAIV refers to live-attenuated influenza vaccine, available as a quadrivalent formulation (LAIV4) since the 2013-2014 season. 19. IIV, RIV, and LAIV denote vaccine categories, with numeric suffixes specifying the number of hemagglutinin (HA) antigens in the vaccine. 20. When necessary to refer specifically to cell culture-based vaccines, the prefix cc is used (e.g., ccIIV4). 21. When necessary to refer specifically to adjuvanted vaccines, the prefix a is used (e.g., aIIV3). 22. Recommendations for influenza vaccination of individuals with egg allergy have been modified, including the removal of the recommendation that egg-allergic recipients be observed for 30 minutes post-vaccination for signs of an allergic reaction. 23. Providers should consider observing all patients for 15 minutes after vaccination to reduce the risk of injury should they experience syncope, as per the ACIP General Recommendations on Immunization. 24. Individuals with a history of severe allergic reaction to egg (any symptom other than hives) should be vaccinated in an inpatient or outpatient medical setting under the supervision of a healthcare provider capable of recognizing and managing severe allergic conditions. 25. Influenza A and B are the two types of influenza viruses that cause epidemic human disease. 26. Influenza A viruses are categorized into subtypes based on the characterization of two surface antigens: hemagglutinin (HA) and neuraminidase (NA). 27. Influenza A (H1N1) viruses, influenza A (H3N2) viruses, and influenza B viruses co-circulate globally. 28. New influenza virus variants emerge due to point mutations and recombination events during viral replication, resulting in frequent antigenic changes (antigenic drift). 29. Immunity to surface antigens, HA and NA, reduces the likelihood of infection. 30. Antibody against one influenza virus type or subtype provides limited or no protection against another type or subtype. 31. Frequent emergence of antigenic variants through antigenic drift is the virologic basis for seasonal epidemics and necessitates consideration for adjustment of vaccine viruses each season. 32. Larger genetic changes, or antigenic shifts, occur less frequently among influenza A viruses but can result in new or substantially different subtypes with the potential to cause pandemics. 33. In April 2009, human infections with a novel influenza A (H1N1) virus caused a worldwide pandemic. 34. This virus was antigenically distinct from human influenza A (H1N1) viruses in circulation from 1977 through spring 2009. 35. Influenza B viruses are separated into two distinct genetic lineages (Yamagata and Victoria) but are not categorized into subtypes. 36. Influenza B viruses undergo antigenic drift less rapidly than influenza A viruses. 37. Influenza B viruses from both lineages have co-circulated in most influenza seasons since the 1980s. 38. Trivalent influenza vaccines available in recent seasons have contained one influenza B virus, representing only one lineage. 39. The proportion of circulating influenza B viruses that are of the lineage represented in the vaccine has varied. 40. During the 10 seasons from 2001-2002 through 2010-2011, the predominant circulating influenza B virus lineage in the United States was represented in the trivalent vaccine in only five seasons. 41. During the 11 seasons from 2004-2005 through 2015-2016 (excluding the 2009 pandemic period), the more prevalent circulating B lineage was represented in the vaccine in eight seasons.
